title: Maternal collapse and resuscitation
blurb: Lead the first minutes of a maternal cardiac arrest: call for help, high-quality CPR, manual uterine displacement, the 4Hs, 4Ts and 4Ps, and early preparation for resuscitative hysterotomy (RCUK 2025).
question: Precious, 33 weeks pregnant, collapses on the antenatal ward. She is unresponsive and not breathing normally. After calling for help and starting CPR, what should the midwife do to make compressions more effective?

teach.body: Formally (Resuscitation Council UK 2025, special circumstances): above 20 weeks' gestation, relieve aortocaval compression as early as possible and maintain it throughout resuscitation. In plain English: once the uterus is big enough, lying flat lets it press on the inferior vena cava and aorta, so very little blood returns to the heart and CPR cannot circulate it. Moving the uterus off those vessels is part of good CPR, not an extra.
teach.cite: RCUK 2025 Special circumstances: cardiac arrest in pregnancy

items: Consider pregnancy in any collapsed woman of childbearing age (RCUK 2025).
Pregnant and postpartum women can deteriorate to arrest anywhere; obstetric early warning systems help spot it early.
Unresponsive and not breathing normally: shout for help and call the emergency team, including obstetric, anaesthetic and neonatal staff.
Start CPR straight away: 30 compressions to 2 breaths, rate 100 to 120 per minute, depth 5 to 6 cm (RCUK 2025 adult BLS and ALS).
Bring the defibrillator and emergency equipment; follow the adult ALS algorithm.

rows.label: How
values: Push the uterus up and to her left
Wedge or tilt the whole body

rows.label: Compressions
values: Woman stays flat on a firm surface

teach.caption: RCUK 2025: manual left uterine displacement is preferred over lateral tilt because of the practicalities of delivering chest compressions. Apply it above 20 weeks.

head: 4Hs
4Ts
4Ps (pregnancy)
teach.caption: RCUK 2025: systematically address the 4Hs and 4Ts and seek pregnancy-specific causes, the 4Ps. Thrombosis and thromboembolism are the leading cause of UK maternal death during or up to 6 weeks after pregnancy (MBRRACE-UK 2022-24).

teach.body: Resuscitative hysterotomy (perimortem caesarean) is a time-sensitive intervention. Prepare for it early, and perform it as soon as possible, at the site of the cardiac arrest, by a skilled team. Emptying the uterus removes aortocaval compression and helps resuscitation of the woman. RCUK 2025 does not set a fixed number of minutes: the message is early preparation and no transfer to theatre.

teach.h: The first minutes of a maternal arrest

teach.caption: Allocate clear roles, including someone to record events and someone to support her partner or family.

teach.h: Scenario: Precious on the antenatal ward
items: Precious, 33 weeks, was admitted with severe pre-eclampsia. The midwife finds her unresponsive and not breathing normally.
She pulls the emergency bell, calls the team and starts chest compressions on a firm surface.
A second midwife displaces the uterus manually up and to the left while CPR continues.
The team leader works through the 4Hs, 4Ts and 4Ps; pre-eclampsia and eclampsia are the obvious P.
The obstetric team prepares for resuscitative hysterotomy on the ward, at the bedside, without moving her.

teach.text: Don't learn a minute number for perimortem caesarean as an RCUK 2025 rule. The current wording is 'time-sensitive': prepare early, do it as soon as possible, at the site of arrest. And don't move a woman in arrest to theatre for it.

items: Consider pregnancy in any collapsed woman of childbearing age.
Above 20 weeks, relieve aortocaval compression early; manual left uterine displacement is preferred over tilt.
Adult CPR: 30:2, 100 to 120 compressions per minute, 5 to 6 cm deep.
Look for 4Hs, 4Ts and the 4Ps: pre-eclampsia/eclampsia, puerperal sepsis, placental/uterine complications, peripartum cardiomyopathy.
Resuscitative hysterotomy: prepare early, perform as soon as possible at the site of arrest.

summary: You can now start and lead the first minutes of a maternal cardiac arrest, explain why and how to relieve aortocaval compression, and work through the 4Hs, 4Ts and 4Ps. You can also describe RCUK 2025 advice on resuscitative hysterotomy and allocate team roles.

A.q: A woman at 30 weeks has a cardiac arrest on the antenatal ward. CPR has started on a firm surface. What does RCUK 2025 recommend to relieve aortocaval compression?
options: Turn her fully onto her right side
A.why: RCUK 2025: manual left uterine displacement is preferred over lateral tilt in maternal cardiac arrest because of the practicalities of delivering chest compressions.

whyNot.0: Leg raising does not move the uterus off the inferior vena cava and aorta.
whyNot.2: A full side position prevents effective chest compressions, and displacement is to the left.
whyNot.3: Head-down tilt does not relieve aortocaval compression.

A.q: Which of these is one of the pregnancy-specific '4Ps' causes of cardiac arrest in RCUK 2025?
A.why: The 4Ps are pre-eclampsia and eclampsia, puerperal sepsis, placental and uterine complications, and peripartum cardiomyopathy.

whyNot.0: Tension pneumothorax is one of the 4Ts, not a pregnancy-specific P.

A.q: Above what gestation does RCUK 2025 advise relieving aortocaval compression during resuscitation?
A.why: RCUK 2025: above 20 weeks' gestation, relieve aortocaval compression as early as possible and maintain it throughout resuscitation.

whyNot.0: At 12 weeks the uterus is still within the pelvis.
whyNot.1: 16 weeks is earlier than the RCUK threshold of 20 weeks.
whyNot.2: Waiting until 28 weeks would miss women between 20 and 28 weeks who are at risk.

B.q: Why does RCUK 2025 prefer manual uterine displacement over a lateral tilt during maternal cardiac arrest?
options: It makes chest compressions easier to deliver
It reduces the risk of aspiration
It gives better access for defibrillation
It lowers the risk of uterine rupture
B.why: RCUK 2025 gives the practicalities of delivering chest compressions as the reason: the woman stays flat on a firm surface.

whyNot.1: Aspiration risk is managed through airway care, not the method of displacement.
whyNot.2: Pad placement is possible with either; this is not the reason given.
whyNot.3: Uterine rupture is not the rationale for choosing displacement over tilt.

B.q: During a maternal cardiac arrest at 36 weeks on the labour ward, where should resuscitative hysterotomy be performed?
options: At the site of the cardiac arrest
B.why: RCUK 2025: resuscitative hysterotomy should be performed as soon as possible, at the site of cardiac arrest, by a skilled team.

whyNot.0: Moving to theatre delays a time-sensitive intervention and interrupts CPR.
whyNot.2: Any transfer delays the procedure; it is done where the arrest happens.

B.q: During adult CPR for a pregnant woman, which compression rate and depth are correct (RCUK 2025)?
B.why: RCUK 2025 adult BLS: compress at 100 to 120 per minute to a depth of at least 5 cm but not more than 6 cm, with a ratio of 30:2.

whyNot.0: Both the rate and the depth are below the adult standard.
whyNot.1: Both the rate and the depth are above the recommended range.
whyNot.2: The rate is right but 3 to 4 cm is too shallow for an adult.

C.q: Tola, 37 weeks, had BP 172/114 and a severe headache before she was found in cardiac arrest. Which of the 4Ps is the most likely cause?
C.why: Severe hypertension with a severe headache before collapse points to pre-eclampsia and eclampsia, one of the RCUK 2025 4Ps.

whyNot.0: Nothing in her history suggests infection.
whyNot.2: There is no history of bleeding or uterine pain to suggest abruption or rupture.
whyNot.3: Cardiomyopathy usually presents with breathlessness and heart failure, not severe hypertension with headache.

C.q: A woman at 34 weeks arrests on the antenatal ward. CPR and uterine displacement are under way and the obstetric team has arrived. What should they do now?
options: Prepare for hysterotomy at the bedside
Move her to theatre for caesarean
Listen for the fetal heart first
Delay surgery until she is stable
C.why: RCUK 2025: resuscitative hysterotomy is time-sensitive; preparation should start early and it is performed as soon as possible at the site of arrest.

whyNot.1: Transfer interrupts CPR and delays a time-sensitive procedure.
whyNot.2: Fetal assessment does not guide maternal resuscitation and wastes time.
whyNot.3: The hysterotomy is done to help resuscitate her; waiting for stability defeats its purpose.

C.q: Twenty minutes after a vaginal birth, Mei collapses with a large pool of blood on the bed. CPR is started. Which reversible cause is most likely?
C.why: Massive bleeding after birth causes hypovolaemia, one of the 4Hs; treating the bleeding and replacing volume is central to her resuscitation.

whyNot.0: Hypothermia is not suggested by a sudden collapse with heavy bleeding.
whyNot.2: There is no history of overdose or drug toxicity.
whyNot.3: Tamponade usually follows trauma or cardiac surgery, not postpartum haemorrhage.

reteach.title: The uterus is sitting on the hose
reteach.question: Picture the inferior vena cava as a garden hose bringing blood back to the heart, and a 30-week uterus sitting on it. What does CPR achieve while it stays there?

blocks.h: Lift the weight off the hose
blocks.body: With the uterus pressing on the vena cava, compressions push very little blood round the body, because little returns to the heart. Pushing the uterus up and to her left lifts it off the hose, and she can stay flat for good compressions. If the woman still does not respond, delivering the baby by resuscitative hysterotomy removes the weight entirely, which is why it is prepared early.

steps.label: Hysterotomy
steps.sub: As soon as possible, at the site

blocks.text: Displacement is to the woman's LEFT, because the vena cava lies to the right of the spine.

explain.body: Consider pregnancy in any collapsed woman of childbearing age. If she is unresponsive and not breathing normally, call for help, including obstetric, anaesthetic and neonatal teams, and start CPR at 30:2 (RCUK 2025).

test.q: A woman of 28 is found collapsed in the hospital car park. According to RCUK 2025, what should responders bear in mind?
options: Pregnancy is unlikely if she is not showing
She could be pregnant or recently pregnant
Check a pregnancy test before CPR
Pregnancy changes the CPR ratio to 15:2
test.why: RCUK 2025: consider pregnancy in any collapsed woman of childbearing age.

whyNot.0: Early pregnancy and recent birth are not visible, so pregnancy must still be considered.
whyNot.2: CPR must never wait for a test; resuscitation starts at once.
whyNot.3: The adult ratio stays at 30:2 in pregnancy.

explain.body: Above 20 weeks, relieve aortocaval compression as early as possible and maintain it throughout. Manual left uterine displacement is preferred over lateral tilt, so compressions can be delivered with the woman flat (RCUK 2025).

test.q: During CPR on a woman at 32 weeks, which action best relieves aortocaval compression while keeping compressions effective?
options: Pushing the uterus up and to her left
Raising the head of the bed
test.why: Manual left uterine displacement keeps the woman flat for compressions while moving the uterus off the great vessels (RCUK 2025).

whyNot.0: Displacement is to the left, and tilt makes compressions harder.
whyNot.1: Knee support does not move the uterus off the vena cava.
whyNot.3: Raising the head does not relieve compression and makes CPR less effective.

explain.body: Work through the 4Hs (hypoxia, hypovolaemia, electrolyte disorders, hypothermia), the 4Ts (thrombosis, tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins) and the 4Ps (pre-eclampsia/eclampsia, puerperal sepsis, placental/uterine complications, peripartum cardiomyopathy).

test.q: A woman 5 days after a caesarean with fever, tachycardia and an offensive wound collapses. Which 4P cause should the team consider first?
test.why: Fever, tachycardia and wound infection after birth point to puerperal sepsis, one of the 4Ps.

whyNot.0: There is no bleeding or uterine complication described.
whyNot.1: There is no hypertension or seizure history.
whyNot.2: Her signs point to infection rather than heart failure.

explain.body: Resuscitative hysterotomy is time-sensitive: prepare early and perform it as soon as possible at the site of arrest by a skilled team. Post-resuscitation care needs a multidisciplinary approach (RCUK 2025).

rows.label: When
values: Waiting to see if CPR works

test.q: Which statement about resuscitative hysterotomy reflects RCUK 2025 guidance?
options: It is delayed until the fetal heart is heard
It is performed after transfer to theatre
It is reserved for gestations over 37 weeks
test.why: RCUK 2025 describes resuscitative hysterotomy as time-sensitive, to be prepared early and performed as soon as possible at the site of arrest.

whyNot.1: It is done to help resuscitate the woman, not dependent on fetal heart findings.
whyNot.2: It is performed at the site of arrest, not after transfer.
whyNot.3: Aortocaval compression matters above 20 weeks, not just at term.
